title: Miss North Carolina USA Winner Says She Never Approved N-Word Apology
paragraphs: Miss North Carolina to Miss USA I Never Apologized for Using N-Word!!!

Miss North Carolina USA winner Brittany Boltinhouse is firing back at the organization's attempt to toss her lawsuit ... insisting she never agreed to apologize for using the n-word in old social media posts.

According to new court docs, obtained by TMZ, Boltinhouse claims CEO Thom Brodeur and other pageant officials falsely portrayed her as admitting to racist misconduct and accepting responsibility through a written apology she never approved.

Brittany acknowledges using the slur in posts from seven years ago ... but insists the apology was drafted by someone else and sent to her for approval, which she says she flatly refused. She says the apology was still falsely presented as hers.

Her attorneys argue there's a big difference between calling someone racist and publicly claiming that person admitted to being racist ... especially when the supposed confession was never authorized.
The filing also refers to her past use of the n-word as slang ... arguing that even if people find the language offensive, that doesn't mean she agreed to the apology attributed to her.

As TMZ previously reported, Brodeur asked the court to dismiss Brittany's defamation lawsuit earlier this month ... arguing the organization's statements were protected opinions and pointing to her admitted use of the slur.
Brittany was stripped of her crown in August after the old posts resurfaced. She later sued, claiming pageant officials also targeted her over her conservative Christian beliefs and political views.

Now, she's asking the court to reject the dismissal attempt ... arguing the dispute isn't about whether Miss USA had the right to dethrone her ... but whether officials had the right to put words in her mouth.

title: Senegal boat disaster: Dozens missing as boat with 100 migrants sinks
paragraphs: Dozens missing after boat carrying 100 migrants sinks off Senegal's coast
Senegalese authorities are continuing search operations after a boat reportedly carrying about 100 migrants capsized off the coast.
Initial reports said that one person had died, but some local media have reported that at least four bodies have been recovered. Dozens of people are still missing.

Personal belongings were found on the badly damaged boat, which washed ashore near the village of Yenne, south of Dakar. Search operations continued throughout Wednesday and were due to resume on Thursday.
This comes less than two weeks after a shipwreck off the coast of the north-western town of Thieppe killed at least 39 people, in one of Senegal's deadliest migration disasters.
Oumar Sow, a representative of the village chief, said the latest tragedy happened around 02:00 local time (02:00 GMT).
"Cries could be heard coming from the pirogue that were audible even from the beach," the AFP news agency quoted him as saying.
A survivor questioned by the police said there were about 100 people on the boat, including five women, AFP reported.
Police recovered identity documents, several mobile phones and personal belongings from the wreckage, including a school enrolment document.
At a cabinet meeting on Wednesday, President Diomaye Faye expressed concern about a renewed increase in irregular departure by migrants hoping to reach Europe.
He instructed the interior ministry to prepare a report examining the factors driving the dangerous journeys and proposing measures to tackle the problem.
Following last month's tragedy, Faye had urged Senegalese people not to risk their lives attempting the dangerous sea crossings.
Many thousands of people from West Africa have died or gone missing trying to flee conflict, authoritarian rule or poverty in recent years.
The UN's migration agency IOM said last month that it had recorded at least 454 deaths and disappearances off the West African coast this year alone.
It warned the figures were likely to be an underestimate, as many boats disappear without leaving survivors or a trace.

As it has become more difficult to reach Europe through North Africa, due to tighter controls and increased co-operation with European countries, migrants are increasingly targeting Spain's Canary Islands.
They often travel in wooden boats known as pirogues that are frequently overloaded and not suited to such long voyages across the Atlantic Ocean.
Most migrants arriving in the Canary Islands this year are from Senegal, according to the UN.
They are driven to leave home by limited employment opportunities, family pressures and established migration networks, according to the IOM.
On 7 November, El Hierro, one of the Canary Islands, declared a state of emergency following a surge in migrant arrivals.
It said more than 3,300 people had reached the island in about 30 boats since the beginning of the month. This amounts to almost a third of the island's population.

title: Ukraine war briefing: Russia asks if Netherlands has joined conflict after Crimea bridge strike
paragraphs: Russia’s embassy in the Netherlands has posted a statement asking if the Netherlands had openly joined ⁠the conflict ⁠in ​Ukraine after a Dutch-based company said its missiles ⁠were used by Kyiv in Tuesday’s attack on a Crimean bridge. A section ​of the Kerch bridge that ‌connects annexed Crimea and Russia was destroyed on Tuesday by waves of ⁠drones and missiles. Soon after, Destinus – a Dutch-headquartered startup – confirmed its Ruta cruise missiles ‌were the only foreign-made weapons used in the attack, a rare operational role for a western manufacturer in a significant long-range strike.

In response to the revelation, the ​Russian embassy said on X that “Moscow has ⁠been duly informed of the NL (Netherlands) involvement”, above a ​statement from ‌Destinus detailing ​its ​role in the bridge attack. The embassy added: “The confession has been well noted. Is The Hague openly joining the conflict?”

In a separate strike on Wednesday, the bridge was attacked again, temporarily halting traffic. “An assessment of the damage is under way,” Sergei Aksyonov, the Moscow-appointed head of Crimea, wrote on Telegram. For Ukraine, the bridge is a hated symbol of Russian arrogance and colonial thinking. Ukraine has previously declared that the bridge across the Kerch strait, built eight years ago, is illegal. The strike came hours ahead of a meeting between Vladimir Putin, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping at Apec in China.

Trump plans to meet separately with Putin on Thursday, in addition to their already scheduled three-way meeting with Xi, a US official confirmed. Trump’s meeting with Putin would be the first time that the leaders have held talks since their discussions in Alaska last year that failed to broker a deal to ease Russia’s war in Ukraine.

A Russian man has been arrested in California for allegedly conducting surveillance of employees of a Silicon Valley technology and defence company that provided assistance to Ukraine, US officials said. The targeted company was not named in the indictment but it was described as a “large, publicly traded” technology and defence company with office locations throughout the US, including in Palo Alto.

Ukraine struck two oil refineries in southern Russia overnight, Ukrainian officials said on Wednesday. Ukraine’s general staff said the strikes hit storage tanks at the Ilsky refinery and a processing unit at the Afipsky refinery, both in Russia’s Krasnodar region. The two refineries, also targeted Sunday night, could together process about 95m barrels of oil a year and supply Russian forces on the frontlines in southern and eastern Ukraine, it said.

Russian drones attacked energy facilities, civilian businesses and residential buildings in five regions overnight and Wednesday morning, Ukrainian prime minister Serhii Koretskyi said. A Russian strike on the southern Ukrainian city of Odesa killed four people, officials said. A Russian drone attack on a market in the Kharkiv region wounded 12 people, including an 11-year-old boy, Ukraine’s State Emergency Services said.

The EU has proposed member states give Ukraine an extra €45bn ($49bn) loan to plug its 2027 budget shortfalls as Russia’s invasion drags on, Jennifer Rankin writes. The funding would fill two-thirds of a €70bn black hole Kyiv faces next year. “We think this is the best way to give Ukraine a strong hand at the negotiation table, and Ukraine only needs to repay once Russia pays for the damage it has caused in Ukraine,” European Commission chief Ursula von der Leyen said. EU leaders will discuss the loan next week.

US diplomatic envoys Steve Witkoff and ⁠Jared Kushner are expected in Berlin on Thursday to meet Ukrainian officials and a European negotiating team, a US official said. The meetings would focus on further developing “credible postwar security guarantees” ⁠for Ukraine, and preparing for the next round of multilateral talks, the official said.

Russian ⁠athletes will not be allowed into ⁠the ⁠Czech Republic, ​which is hosting ⁠the women’s under-18 ice hockey world championship ⁠in January. In comments to local media, interior minister ‌Lubomir Metnar ‌reiterated his government would not ‌be issuing visas for Russian ​athletes. He added that the ministry also had ⁠legal instruments to ​prevent entry for ​athletes ​receiving visas from ​other ‌states ​in ​Europe’s border-free Schengen zone.

title: AI giant Anthropic raises more than $100 billion in record-setting IPO
paragraphs: Anthropic shares are about to make their market debut after the company raised more than $100 billion in a record-breaking initial public offering that valued it at around $1.5 trillion.
It's a remarkably rapid ascent for the five-year-old artificial intelligence powerhouse, and a sign of strong investor appetite despite growing concern about a possible AI bubble.
Anthropic sold 956 million shares — far more than originally planned — at an IPO price of $83 per share, it announced on Wednesday. That price exceeded its targeted range of $70 to $78 per share.

The company's seven founders also sold more than 23 million shares as part of the IPO. On top of that, Anthropic's prospectus included plans to put an additional $26 billion worth of shares into the market through private placements with companies including Google, Microsoft and Nvidia.
The total haul is more than $107 billion.
Anthropic valuation could rise or fall later on Thursday, when its shares start trading publicly on the Nasdaq exchange under the ticker symbol ANT.
The amount of money raised makes Anthropic's IPO the biggest in history, after Elon Musk's mega-conglomerate SpaceX landed $75 billion when it listed in June.
A breakaway beginning
Anthropic's rise has been meteoric.
"We've never seen a company that's able to grow this fast [and] be this dominant," said Andrew Rocco, a stock analyst at the financial research firm Zacks.

Anthropic got its start in 2021 as a breakaway group of researchers who once worked for ChatGPT-maker OpenAI. Led by now-CEO Dario Amodei, the Anthropic founders were concerned that OpenAI, run by Sam Altman, was not on a path to develop AI safely.

Amodei and the others quickly raised hundreds of millions of dollars and set out to develop AI models in a way that the company said focused on safety and "alignment," or the idea that AI should be harmless and act in ways that jibe with human values and intent.

Anthropic launched Claude in early 2023, just months after OpenAI released ChatGPT. Ever since, the two companies have been neck-and-neck competitors in cutting-edge artificial intelligence, known as "frontier AI." The Claude family of AI models, including the Claude chatbot and Claude Code, are among the most popular and powerful in the world, and have helped transform everything from online search to software engineering.

They are also the San Francisco-based company's main source of income, according to its IPO prospectus, which said revenue in the first half of the year skyrocketed 1,300% at $16.3 billion, while its adjusted operating income — a measure of potential profitability — hit $1.6 billion during the period, versus a loss of $1.8 billion the year before.
Opportunities and risks

The IPO comes at a time when shares in tech companies linked to the AI boom have been volatile. Investors have vacillated between enthusiasm for what many believe will be a revolutionary technology and concern that the vast sums of money being poured into it may be hard to justify.

"It's going to be a test of investor sentiment towards the AI trade," said Janice Quek, an equity analyst at the investment research firm CFRA. "We've seen in recent weeks that there has been a lot of pressure and really market sell-offs on the AI ecosystem just because a lot of people are worried about the AI bubble, for example, or the concerns around AI financing and whether there's a return on investment on AI."
The tech-heavy Nasdaq is down more than 11% since early October.

Altimeter Capital CEO Brad Gerstner, an early Anthropic investor, told a Semafor conference on Monday the IPO is one of the best ways to invest in AI applications. He said his firm had trimmed its exposure to AI infrastructure — companies involved in things like manufacturing semiconductors and building data centers — but that Altimeter had requested an allotment of Anthropic stock worth $5 billion.
"I've been waiting for it," he said of the IPO. "We put in for the largest request in the 20-year history of our firm."

There is indirect evidence in Anthropic's prospectus that businesses, rather than individual subscribers, are its biggest source of revenue. Malik Ahmed Khan, an equity analyst at Morningstar, says the company's long-term success may hinge on those companies' pace of adoption of AI technologies, but it's unclear how fast that will be.

"Radios went from like 10% penetration to 90% penetration in the U.S. within a decade. Washing machines, to reach that level of penetration, took a multi-decade period," he said. "So when we're thinking about Anthropic and broadly AI in the enterprise setting, what does that adoption curve look like?"
Conflict with the Pentagon, and "pacing the frontier"

Anthropic has not been without controversy. Earlier this year it became embroiled in a conflict with the Pentagon over how its models can be used. The Pentagon wanted the military to be able to deploy Anthropic's models without restriction, but Amodei drew a line at fully autonomous weapons and mass surveillance of Americans. The Pentagon subsequently labeled Anthropic a "supply chain risk," a designation previously reserved for foreign adversaries.

And skeptics have criticized Amodei's rapid push to develop AI despite his own dire warnings about the technology's risks. In September, Amodei wrote an essay urging his AI competitors to "pace the frontier," or to slow down development of the most cutting-edge models and make sure that safety incidents are being reported and scrutinized by third-party auditors.

That essay followed a summer when AI agents from Anthropic's lab, as well as OpenAI and other competitors, were revealed to have hacked other companies, setting off a frenzy of concern about the risks of rogue agents. This week, California sued OpenAI over its agents that hacked into Hugging Face, an open-source software platform.
Anthropic's IPO prospectus dedicated dozens of pages to potential risks, including the possibility that people could lose control of AI, or that AI could take harmful actions on its own.

The company also flagged the risk of heightened scrutiny or political backlash. Indeed, the IPO comes just weeks after midterm elections in the United States, which analysts say likely herald a period of elevated scrutiny and oversight for AI firms. Data centers became a hot-button issue this election cycle, and tech stocks sank after the election as investors anticipated that the incoming Congress would crack down on the industry.

Still, Anthropic's prospectus was bullish about the development and spread of AI. "We believe this abundance of AI will rapidly transform every sector of the global economy in ways greater than the impact of industrialization, electricity, semiconductors, and the internet," it said.

OpenAI had been on track to also list shares this year, but CEO Sam Altman postponed those plans, likely to next year, after the Hugging Face incident. At the Semafor conference on Monday Altman promised: "We will go public at some point."
"The world as a whole would like exposure to this," he continued. "And I think that's, you know, directionally a good thing to do."

Meanwhile, shares in SpaceX, the first of this year's AI mega-IPOs, are trading near their initial price of $135. After the company's June listing, the stock leapt to more than $200, then slid to as low as about $108 before recovering ground.
Anthropic is a financial supporter of NPR.
